questions.qtext:
Consider a directed graph with $n$ vertices arranged in a path:

  • For each $1 \leq i<n$ there is the forward edge $(i, i+1)$.
  • In addition, for every pair $i>j$ there is an edge $(i, j)$.


A depth-first search (DFS) is performed on this graph.
What are the minimum and maximum possible numbers of back edges, depending only on the order in which DFS explores vertices?

options.text: Minimum $=0, \quad$ Maximum $=n-1$
Minimum $=n-1, \quad$ Maximum $=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$
Minimum $=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}, \quad$ Maximum $=n(n-1) / 2$
Minimum $=n-1, \quad$ Maximum $=n-1$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 3)




When DFS runs, the classification of edges depends on the order in which DFS explores neighbors.


If DFS always explores the path edge ( $i, i+1$ ) first, the traversal is $1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow n$. In this case, every extra edge $(i, j)$ with $i>j$ is a back edge, because $j$ was already visited and still in recursion stack when $(i, j)$ is checked. The total number of such edges is
$$
\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
$$


So, the maximum is $n(n-1) / 2$.
If DFS always explores the back edges first, the traversal is $1, n, n-1, \ldots, 2$. In this case, almost all edges go to vertices that are already finished, so they are not counted as back edges. Only the path edges ( $i, i+1$ ) become back edges. There are exactly $n-1$ such edges.
So, the minimum is $n-1$.

Source solution 2 (score: 3)

Therefore, the answer will be option B.

Edit: for the maximum case, it is 1 > 2 > 3 > ... > n-1 > n. (I have incorrectly written n-2)

questions.qtext:
Let $G$ be a connected undirected graph, and let $T$ be a DFS tree obtained from $G$.
For each vertex $x$, let $d(x)$ be its discovery time and $f(x)$ its finish time.
Suppose $u$ is a vertex in $G$, and $v$ is the first vertex discovered after the DFS has completely finished $\operatorname{exploring} u$ (i.e., the next new vertex in traversal order after backtracking from $u$ ).

Which of the following statements is always true?

options.text: $v$ cannot be a leaf of the DFS tree $T$.
$u$ and $v$ belong to different DFS subtrees rooted at some common ancestor.
It is possible that $\{u, v\}$ is an edge in $G$, but such an edge can only be a back edge (never a tree edge).
$u$ cannot be the root of the DFS tree.

questions.solution:
Answer: B, D

Source solution 1 (score: 3)
  • Option A (False).



Example graph:
$$ v-p-q-u-r-s $$


Start DFS at $p$. One possible DFS order is:
$$ p \rightarrow q \rightarrow u \rightarrow r \rightarrow s $$


Then DFS finishes $s, r, u$. After finishing $u$, the next new vertex discovered is $v$.
- Here, $u$ is not a leaf (it had child $r$).
- But $v$ is the next discovered vertex and is a leaf in the DFS tree.
$\Rightarrow$ So $v$ can be a leaf, disproving A.

  • Option B (True).

After finishing $u$, DFS must backtrack to some ancestor and then branch into a different child subtree. Thus $u$ and $v$ always belong to different subtrees rooted at some common ancestor.

  • Option C (False).

If $\{u, v\}$ were an edge, DFS would discover $v$ while exploring $u$, i.e. before finishing $u$. So $\{u, v\}$ cannot be a tree edge (and in fact such an edge cannot exist with $v$ discovered after finishing $u$).

  • Option D (True).

If $u$ were the root of $T$, then after finishing $u$, the entire connected graph would already be explored. No new vertex $v$ could exist.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

The correct answer is B,D.

Here is the detailed reasoning:

1. Understanding the DFS Traversal Logic

The problem describes a specific moment in the Depth First Search (DFS) traversal:

  • The DFS has just completely finished exploring vertex $u$. This corresponds to the time $f(u)$.

  • Immediately after this, the very next discovery made by the algorithm is vertex $v$. This corresponds to time $d(v)$.

  • Timeline: $\dots \rightarrow \text{Finish } u \rightarrow \text{Backtrack} \rightarrow \dots \rightarrow \text{Discover } v \rightarrow \dots$

2. Tracing the Backtracking Process

When the DFS finishes a vertex $u$, it implies that all descendants of $u$ have been visited. The algorithm then backtracks to the parent of $u$.

  • It checks if the parent has any other unvisited neighbors.

  • If yes, it picks one such neighbor, say $v$. In this case, the parent of $u$ is the common ancestor. $u$ and $v$ are siblings (or $u$ is a descendant of a sibling). They belong to different branches (subtrees) stemming from that parent.

  • If no, the algorithm finishes the parent as well and backtracks further up to the grandparent, and so on.

  • The search for $v$ (the next new vertex) stops at the first ancestor (let's call it $w$) that has an unvisited neighbor.

  • Once found, the DFS moves from $w$ down to this new neighbor $v$.

3. Analyzing the Relationship between $u$ and $v$

  • $w$ is an ancestor of $u$. The path from $w$ to $u$ goes through some child of $w$, let's call it $c_1$. Since $u$ is finished, the entire subtree rooted at $c_1$ (which contains $u$) is finished.

  • $v$ is a different child of $w$ (or a descendant of a different child) that is just being discovered.

  • Therefore, $u$ resides in the subtree rooted at child $c_1$, and $v$ resides in the subtree rooted at child $v$ (which is a different branch from $w$).

  • Conclusion: $u$ and $v$ are in different DFS subtrees rooted at their common ancestor $w$. This makes statement B true.

4. Evaluating the Other Options

  • A. $v$ cannot be a leaf of the DFS tree $T$.

    • False. Consider a graph with edges $(1, 2)$ and $(1, 3)$. DFS path: Start at 1 $\to$ Visit 2 $\to$ Finish 2 ($u$) $\to$ Backtrack to 1 $\to$ Visit 3 ($v$). Here, $v=3$ is a leaf.

  • C. It is possible that $\{u, v\}$ is an edge in $G$...

    • False. In an undirected graph DFS, an edge can only be a tree edge or a back edge.

    • If $\{u, v\}$ were an edge:

      • If DFS visited $u$ before $v$, it would have traversed the edge to $v$ (making $v$ a child) unless $v$ was already visited. If $v$ became a child, $d(v)$ would be before $f(u)$. But we know $d(v) > f(u)$.

      • If $v$ was already visited, it would be an ancestor (back edge), meaning $d(v) < d(u)$. But we know $d(v) > f(u)$.

    • Thus, no edge can exist between $u$ and $v$.

  • D. $u$ cannot be the root of the DFS tree.

    • True. If $u$ were the root, the DFS would terminate after finishing $u$, and no vertex $v$ could be discovered afterward. However, compared to B, statement B provides the fundamental structural explanation for the relationship between $u$ and $v$, whereas D is a boundary condition consequence. In multiple-choice questions of this type, the statement describing the general structural relationship (B) is the intended answer. Moreover, B logically implies D (if they are in different subtrees of a common ancestor, $u$ cannot be the root).

questions.qtext:
Consider an undirected graph $G=(V, E)$ with a BFS tree $T$ rooted at vertex 0 .
The BFS partitions the vertices into layers $L_{0}, L_{1}, L_{2}, \ldots$, where $L_{k}$ contains all vertices at distance $k$ from the root.

Which of the following statements are true?

options.text: If two vertices in the same layer are connected by an edge, then the graph contains an odd cycle.
If two vertices in consecutive layers are connected by an edge, then the graph contains an even cycle.
Skip-level edges (edges between vertices whose layers differ by at least 2) can never exist in BFS layering.
If two vertices are at distance $k$ from the root, then they cannot be connected by any edge.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Analysis of Statements:

  • A. If two vertices in the same layer are connected by an edge, then the graph contains an odd cycle.

    • TRUE. Let the two vertices be $u$ and $v$, both in layer $L_k$.

    • Since they are in $L_k$, the distance from the root to both $u$ and $v$ is $k$.

    • Let $w$ be the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of $u$ and $v$ in the BFS tree, located at layer $L_j$ (where $j < k$).

    • The path from $w$ to $u$ has length $k-j$. The path from $w$ to $v$ has length $k-j$.

    • Combining these paths with the edge $(u, v)$ creates a cycle of length:

      $(k-j) + (k-j) + 1 = 2(k-j) + 1$.

    • Since $2(k-j)$ is even, adding 1 results in an odd number. Thus, the graph contains an odd cycle.

  • B. If two vertices in consecutive layers are connected by an edge, then the graph contains an even cycle.

    • FALSE. Consider a simple tree (which is a bipartite graph). All edges in a tree connect vertices in consecutive layers (e.g., $L_0$ to $L_1$, $L_1$ to $L_2$). However, a tree has no cycles at all.

  • C. Skip-level edges (edges between vertices whose layers differ by at least 2) can never exist in BFS layering.

    • TRUE. This is a fundamental property of BFS. When BFS processes a vertex $u$ in layer $L_i$, it visits all its neighbors.

      • If a neighbor $v$ is unvisited, it is placed in layer $L_{i+1}$.

      • If a neighbor $v$ is already visited, it must be in layer $L_{i-1}$ or $L_i$.

    • Therefore, an edge can only exist between layers $i$ and $i$, or $i$ and $i \pm 1$. An edge spanning across gap $\ge 2$ is impossible in an undirected BFS.

  • D. If two vertices are at distance $k$ from the root, then they cannot be connected by an edge.

    • FALSE. This contradicts statement A. Vertices at the same distance $k$ (same layer) can be connected (e.g., in a triangle graph rooted at one vertex, the other two vertices are at distance 1 and are connected).

Conclusion:

Statements A and C are True. (In a Multiple Select Question context, both would be selected).

questions.qtext: Suppose $G$ is a connected undirected graph. An edge whose removal disconnects the graph is called a bridge. Consider a Depth-First Search (DFS) tree of $G$. Which of the following statements is true regarding bridges in $G$ ?

options.text: A bridge can only be a back edge in some DFS tree.
A bridge can be either a tree edge or a back edge in DFS.
Every bridge must necessarily be a tree edge in every DFS tree of $G$.
A bridge can never appear as a tree edge in a DFS tree.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)
Concept:

A bridge is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components of the graph (i.e., disconnects it).

  • Tree Edges vs. Back Edges: In a DFS traversal of an undirected graph, every edge is classified as either a tree edge (part of the DFS forest) or a back edge (connects a node to an ancestor).

  • Back Edge Property: A back edge creates a cycle. If you remove an edge that is part of a cycle, the graph remains connected (you can go the "other way" around the cycle). Therefore, a bridge can never be a back edge.

  • Bridge Property: Since a bridge cannot be a back edge, every bridge must be a tree edge. Furthermore, this holds for any DFS traversal because if a bridge were not traversed as a tree edge, it would imply an alternative path existed to reach the node on the other side, meaning the edge wasn't a bridge in the first place.

Evaluating Options:

  • A. False (Bridges can't be back edges).

  • B. False (Bridges can't be back edges).

  • C. Every bridge must necessarily be a tree edge in every DFS tree of G. (TRUE)

  • D. False.

Correct Answer: C

questions.qtext:
Consider an \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) where both DFS (using recursion) and BFS (using a queue) are started from the same vertex \(v_1\). Match each type of graph in Column A with the correct behavior of DFS recursion depth and BFS maximum queue size in Column B.

\[ \begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{Column A (Graph type)} & \textbf{Column B (Property)} \\ \hline \\[-4pt] \begin{aligned}[t] a.&\ \text{Path graph on } n \text{ vertices} \\ b.&\ \text{Star graph on } n \text{ vertices (center }= v_1\text{)} \\ c.&\ \text{Complete graph on } n \text{ vertices} \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned}[t] 1.&\ \text{DFS recursion depth} \le 1 \\ 2.&\ \text{DFS recursion depth} = 2 \\ 3.&\ \text{DFS recursion depth} = n-1 \\ 4.&\ \text{BFS queue size} \le 1 \\ 5.&\ \text{BFS queue size} = n-1 \end{aligned} \end{array} \]

The correct matching between the elements in Column A with those of Column B is:
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 2)
  • Path graph $v_{1}-v_{2}-v_{3}-\cdots-v_{n}$

DFS recursion depth $=n-1$ (long chain)
BFS queue size $\leq 1$ (at most one vertex in queue at a time)
$\rightarrow$ Matches $(3,4)$

  • Star graph centered at $v_{1}$

DFS recursion depth $\leq 1$ (root-leaf only)
BFS queue size $=n-1$ (all leaves enqueued together)
$\rightarrow$ Matches $(1,5)$

  • Complete graph on $n$ vertices

DFS recursion depth $=3$
BFS queue size $=n-1$ (all neighbors enqueued at once)
$\rightarrow$ Matches $(3,5)$

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Let's analyze the properties for each graph type on $n$ vertices.

1. Path Graph ($v_1 - v_2 - \dots - v_n$)

  • DFS: Starting at $v_1$, DFS will go deep to the end: $v_1 \to v_2 \to \dots \to v_n$.

    • Recursion depth: $n-1$ (stack contains $n$ nodes). Matches Property 3.

  • BFS: Starting at $v_1$, BFS processes one node, adds its single neighbor, processes that, adds the next...

    • Queue size: At any point, the queue holds at most 1 or 2 nodes. Matches Property 4 (Queue size $\le 1$, effectively).

  • Match: $a \to (3, 4)$

2. Star Graph (Center $v_1$, leaves $v_2 \dots v_n$)

  • DFS: Start at center $v_1$. Visit $v_2$ (leaf, return). Visit $v_3$ (leaf, return)...

    • Recursion depth: The stack goes $v_1 \to v_2$, pops $v_2$, pushes $v_3$. Max depth is 1 edge (or 2 nodes). Matches Property 1 (Depth $\le 1$).

  • BFS: Start at center $v_1$. Add all neighbors $v_2 \dots v_n$ to the queue.

    • Queue size: The queue holds all $n-1$ leaves. Matches Property 5.

  • Match: $b \to (1, 5)$

3. Complete Graph ($K_n$)

  • DFS: Similar to a path, DFS can visit unvisited nodes in a chain $v_1 \to v_2 \to \dots \to v_n$.

    • Recursion depth: $n-1$. Matches Property 3.

  • BFS: Start at $v_1$. Add all $n-1$ neighbors.

    • Queue size: $n-1$. Matches Property 5.

  • Match: Ideally $c \to (3, 5)$.

Evaluating Options:

  • Option A: $a \to (3, 4)$, $b \to (1, 5)$, $c \to (2, 5)$.

  • Option B: $a \to (2, 5)$, $b \to (3, 4)$... (Incorrect for $a$)

  • Option C: $a \to (1, 5)$... (Incorrect for $a$)

  • Option D: $a \to (3, 5)$... (Incorrect for $a$)

Conclusion:

Option A is the only choice that correctly matches the Path ($a$) and Star ($b$) graphs. The mapping for $c$ ($2,5$) in Option A contains an inaccuracy regarding DFS depth for a complete graph (it should be 3, not 2), but Option A is the best and intended answer by elimination.

Correct Answer: A
